newsitem.title: UK: N.Sea Maureen platform set for second lease on life.
newsitem.headline: N.Sea Maureen platform set for second lease on life.

text.p: Recycling is the environmentally-friendly solution to the decommissioning of the North Sea's Maureen oil production platform, but it is not an option open to other oil companies grappling with the touchy subject of platform disposal, Maureen operator Phillips Petroleum Co said.

Maureen is the only fixed platform in the world designed to be refloated and put back into use elsewhere when the field's productive life is over, David Brown, exploitation and development manager of Phillips Petroleum Co UK Ltd, told a press briefing in Aberdeen.
"The whole platform is designed to be floated out and reused," he said.
Maureen lies about 260 kilometres northeast of Aberdeen in Block 16/29a in the U.K. sector of the North Sea.
The field came onstream in 1983 and reached peak production of 102,000 barrels per day (bpd) in 1984. Output is now 10,000 bpd, and production is expected to cease between 1998 and the year 2000.
Phillips has embarked on worldwide marketing push to try and find a new home for the steel gravity structure, Brown said.

The platform currently operates in water depths of 95 meters and could be used in minimum depths of 65 to 70 metres, making it suitable for production in the North Sea, offshore Alaska, the Gulf of Mexico, the Mediterranean, in areas off East Africa, New Zealand and Australia, or in the waters around Indonesia and Malaysia, he said.
The initial investment in the platform was $1 billion, but Brown would not be drawn on its second hand value.
"It's a good marketable commodity and we are even developing opportunities ourselves for it," he said.
Phillips said that studies have shown that the platform could be lifted from the sea bed and floated by filling the three storage tanks, each with a capacity of 220,000 barrels of oil, with air.
"It's a platform that's ready to go. It's very stable when you're towing it," Brown added.

Elsewhere in the North Sea, the Heather and NW Hutton fields are also coming to the end of their working lives and their operators are considering options for decommissioning. Unocal Corp is the operator of Heather and Amoco Corp of NW Hutton.

"Most attention is on them as they are closest to ceasing production...studies have already been commissioned," said David Rodger, project manager of the Offshore Decommissioning Communications Project (ODCP).

He said that the uncertainties surrounding decommissioning of offshore installations in the wake of the Brent Spar debacle gave companies an incentive to keep production going for as long as possible.

In 1995, Royal Dutch/Shell Group was forced to abandon plans to ditch the Brent Spar platform in the Atlantic after environmental group Greenpeace launched a high profile campaign including a boycott of Shell petrol stations in Germany.
